strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation across 17 real-world datasets, multiple ablation variants (a,b,c), synthetic simulations (homo/heteroskedastic, multivariate), and a detailed case study (Ames Housing) examining how uncertainty allocation shifts with feature availability.

The core idea of decoupling the calibration scale (γ1) from the aleatoric/epistemic weighting ratio (λ) is a sensible and well-motivated generalization of prior work that fixes λ=1 (Deep Ensembles, MC-Dropout, Bayesian methods) or γ1=1 (UACQR), and the paper provides a thorough taxonomy of related work explaining this gap.

Asymptotic conditional coverage is proven (Lemma 2.1) and a finite-sample marginal coverage guarantee is provided for a 'conformalized' variant in the appendix, giving the method some theoretical grounding despite the impossibility results for exact finite-sample conditional coverage.

The empirical improvements (double-digit % reductions in NCIW/quantile loss versus individually-calibrated CQR/PCS baselines, and consistent gains over UACQR) are reasonably robust across three different base-model configurations, suggesting the method is not overly tuned to one setup.
The residual-based CQR variant (ALEATORIC-R) is a useful and clearly demonstrated practical improvement in its own right, independent of the main CLEAR contribution.

Good transparency: extensive appendices with per-dataset tables, standard deviations across seeds, and honest discussion of limitations (calibration set reuse, computational overhead, structural additivity assumption).
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is somewhat incremental: it amounts to a two-parameter (multiplicative scale + mixing ratio) conformal calibration on top of pre-existing epistemic (PCS) and aleatoric (CQR/quantile regression) estimators, optimized via grid search on a validation set, which is conceptually close to prior work (UACQR) with one additional degree of freedom.

The default implementation reuses the validation/calibration set both for selecting λ and calibrating γ1 (and often also for base-model selection), which breaks the standard conformal exchangeability argument for finite-sample marginal coverage; the paper acknowledges this and offers a fixed 'Conformalized CLEAR' variant only in the appendix, with the main text relying on an asymptotic argument and empirical PICP checks rather than a rigorous finite-sample guarantee for the actual method used in experiments.

Absolute magnitude of gains in the more 'fair' ablations (variant b, which restricts all methods to the same single base model) is modest in several datasets (e.g., only 3-5% NCIW improvement over ALEATORIC-R in variant a/b), suggesting much of the headline improvement comes from the auxiliary residual-based CQR contribution rather than the λ/γ1 decoupling itself.

No empirical comparison to deep-learning-based joint aleatoric/epistemic estimators (Deep Ensembles, MC-Dropout, BNNs) despite an extensive theoretical discussion of them in the appendix; all real-data experiments are restricted to tree/quantile-regression-based PCS ensembles, limiting the generality of the empirical claims.

The λ grid search (over 4000 points) combined with quantile-loss selection on a validation set introduces additional hyperparameter search overhead and a risk of overfitting to the validation set, especially for smaller datasets; the paper's mitigation ("a limited size of validation set can lead to overfitting") is acknowledged as a limitation without a systematic quantitative study of how validation set size affects reliability.

The computational cost of the full pipeline (bootstrapped PCS ensembles with b=100, combined with bootstrapped residual quantile regression) is nontrivial and only briefly discussed as a limitation, without wall-clock timing comparisons against simpler baselines.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: existing approaches typically combine aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty with a fixed ratio (λ=1) or fixed γ1=1, which the paper shows can be substantially suboptimal; the two-parameter calibration (γ1, γ2=λγ1) is a simple but sensible generalization.

Extremely thorough empirical evaluation: 17 real-world datasets, multiple ablation variants (a/b/c) isolating the effect of base-model choice, additional validation with Deep Ensembles + SQR to show generality beyond PCS/CQR, synthetic homoskedastic/heteroskedastic/multivariate simulations, a real case study (Ames housing) showing adaptive behavior of λ under varying information content, and reported runtimes showing negligible overhead of the calibration step.

Reasonable theoretical grounding: finite-sample marginal coverage guarantee for a 'conformalized CLEAR' variant, an asymptotic conditional-coverage result (Theorem/Lemma 2.1) under consistency assumptions, and an extensive discussion of the properties of the quantile loss as a proper scoring rule with several illustrative counterexamples showing why NCIW/PICP alone can be misleading.

Strong and unusually comprehensive treatment of related work (Appendix A), explicitly situating CLEAR relative to UACQR, Deep Ensembles, MC Dropout, Bayesian NNs, GPR, EPICSCORE, TabPFN, credal sets, etc., with quantitative comparisons where possible.
Good reproducibility support: explicit algorithms (Algorithm 1 and 2), detailed hyperparameter tables, dataset statistics, and metric definitions provided in the appendix.

Consistent and fairly large empirical improvements over strong baselines (calibrated PCS, CQR variants) across most datasets and metrics, with the proposed residual-based aleatoric estimator (ALEATORIC-R) also being a useful independent contribution.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is somewhat limited: it largely amounts to a two-parameter (grid-search-based) conformal calibration on top of existing epistemic (PCS/DE) and aleatoric (CQR/SQR) estimators; the conceptual leap from fixed λ=1 or γ1=1 to jointly tuned (γ1, λ) is intuitive and incremental rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The default (non-conformalized) CLEAR procedure re-uses the validation set as the calibration set and jointly optimizes two parameters on it, which breaks the standard conformal exchangeability argument; the paper acknowledges this and provides a 'Conformalized CLEAR' variant with proper guarantees, but the main results in the body use the less rigorous version, and the practical difference/overfitting risk under small calibration sets is not deeply quantified (only briefly discussed as a limitation).

The comparison against UACQR (closest related method, γ1=1 fixed) may inherently favor CLEAR since it optimizes an additional free parameter on the same objective; while test-set generalization is reported and differences appear robust, a more controlled study of overfitting risk from optimizing 2 vs 1 parameters (e.g., across calibration-set sizes) would strengthen the claim.

Theoretical guarantees (Theorem 2.1, Hypothesis B.8) are somewhat soft: the asymptotic conditional coverage argument relies on generic consistency of base learners and a compact grid, essentially inheriting standard CQR asymptotics; Hypothesis B.8 (finite-sample undercoverage of CQR in extrapolation) is explicitly left as an unproven conjecture, and much of the theoretical appendix is intuitive/discursive rather than rigorous.

The paper is extremely long, with the appendix substantially larger than the main text and containing significant conceptual content (e.g., Appendix I on relative/absolute uncertainty, extensive philosophical discussion in B.4) that arguably belongs in the main paper or a separate treatment; this makes it hard to assess the core contribution in isolation and may frustrate reviewers/readers expecting a self-contained main text.

Computational cost of the primary CLEAR instantiation (100 bootstraps × multiple candidate model classes for PCS, plus a similarly bootstrapped residual QR) is nontrivial for large datasets (e.g., superconductor takes over 1300s for variant (a) baselines combined), which could limit applicability to very large-scale or streaming settings despite claims of parallelizability.

Some empirical claims rely on relatively coarse significance reporting (mean ± std over 10 seeds without formal significance testing), and improvements on certain datasets are modest, with the method occasionally underperforming baselines on specific metrics/datasets (e.g., some 'γ1=1' or 'λ=1' ablations match or slightly beat full CLEAR).
